snippet.title: Inside Nigeria’s Strictest Film Industry | Unreported World
snippet.description:
Unreported World is from Nigeria, home to one of the world’s most prolific film industries.

Reporter Anja Popp meets the women risking their livelihood and reputations to push the boundaries on screen.
 
In the conservative northern city of Kano, Kannywood produces movies for more than 80 million Hausa speakers. But the region is governed by strict Sharia law, and actresses and filmmakers face intense censorship and moral scrutiny.
 
On a rowdy set Popp meets pioneering director Mansurah Isah, one of the industry’s few female directors. Determined to reflect the challenges of Hausa women in a male dominated world, we observe Mansurah anguishing over a childbirth scene that risks being cut for showing too much of a woman’s body.
 
Under Kannywood’s religious restrictions, actresses can also fall foul of the censors, and conservative family expectations. For rising star Amina Shehu, choosing to act has meant losing her family’s support.
 
Yet in southern Nigeria’s booming Nollywood, women are box office powerhouses, though they too say success demands relentless resilience in a male-dominated culture.
 
Director: Stefania Buonajuti
Picture Editor: Einav Leshetz
Series Producer: Andy Lee
Executive Producer: Ed Fraser
Production Company: Channel 4 News

snippet.title: The incredible engineering of Venice - Stephanie H. Smith
snippet.description:
Explore the history of Venice to find out how the infamous floating city was built and how the republic became a hub for trade.

--

To escape Germanic invaders, people fled into the Venetian Lagoon in the 6th century. The settlers set out to tame the mudflats and built a foundation in the marshy maze to support heavier, longer-lasting structures. Little did they know, this system of wood, water, and mud would still be supporting an infamous floating city 1,500 years later. Stephanie H. Smith explores the history of Venice.

snippet.title: The German Gun That Refused To Die! | WWII Normandy
snippet.description:
On D-Day, as thousands of British troops stormed Gold Beach, one German gun position threatened to change the course of the invasion.

Hidden near Le Hamel, an 88mm gun and its determined crew unleashed devastating fire against the landing forces. Destroying tanks, smashing landing craft, and pinning soldiers on the beach, this single weapon became one of the most feared German positions facing the British assault on 6 June 1944.

In this video, we uncover the dramatic story of the Le Hamel 88mm gun, the men who served it, and the desperate efforts made by British troops to silence it. Using battlefield footage, wartime records, veteran accounts, and modern-day exploration, we'll examine how close this gun came to disrupting the assault on Gold Beach and why its story remains one of the most remarkable episodes of D-Day.

Could one gun really have changed the outcome of the invasion?

Join us as we investigate the weapon that almost stopped the British advance on Gold Beach.

The British Walked Straight Into a Deadly Trap at Concord... but what happened next has been debated for more than 250 years.

On 19 April 1775, after the fighting at Lexington and Concord, British regulars began their long retreat to Boston. Along the road, thousands of colonial militia and minutemen emerged from the woods, stone walls and farms, turning the withdrawal into one of the most relentless running battles in military history.

But beyond the famous firefights lies a darker story.

Were British soldiers really scalped after the battle? Were Native American-style tactics used against the King's troops? And how did this brutal ambush shape the opening days of the American Revolutionary War?

In this video, we examine the historical evidence surrounding the Concord ambush, separating documented fact from later myth. Using eyewitness accounts, military reports and contemporary sources, we'll explore how the British column became trapped, why the retreat descended into chaos, and what really happened to the men who fell along the Battle Road.

snippet.title: Kristin Chenoweth Discovers Her 1850s “Hustler” Ancestor | Finding Your Roots
snippet.description:
When I sat down with Kristin Chenoweth on Finding Your Roots, we uncovered a delightful surprise buried in the pages of an 1850 Texas newspaper.

There, in an advertisement from Galveston’s Semi Weekly Journal, was evidence of one of Kristin’s enterprising ancestors promoting his oyster house by invoking the name of the world-famous soprano Jenny Lind, the “Swedish Nightingale.” Whether Lind ever set foot in Galveston is doubtful—but Kristin’s ancestor clearly understood the art of publicity.

What we discovered next was even more revealing: this same man ran a restaurant, raised a family, and served as a lighthouse keeper. In him we see the qualities that so often echo across generations—ambition, adaptability, and a bit of entrepreneurial flair.

It is always remarkable to see how the spirit of performance and perseverance can travel through time, resurfacing in the life of a Broadway star nearly two centuries later.

snippet.title: What Forensics Found in a Gettysburg Sniper’s Attic | Civil War (No AI)
snippet.description:
What happened inside the Shriver House attic during the Battle of Gettysburg?

As Confederate sharpshooters occupied the Shriver family home, they knocked firing holes through the brick walls to target Union soldiers on Cemetery Hill—turning a civilian attic into a deadly sniper position.

More than 160 years later, a modern forensic investigation returned to this Gettysburg sniper nest. Using chemiluminescent blood reagents, investigators confirmed what had long been dismissed as legend: bloodstains from the battle still remained embedded in the attic floorboards.

This is the story of the Shriver House sniper nest—and the scientific evidence that proved it was real.

snippet.title: Surviving Earth's Most Extreme Climates (Full Episode) | Hostile Planet: Compilation | Nat Geo
snippet.description:
Hosted by Bear Grylls, Hostile Planet zooms in on the world’s most extreme environments to reveal the animal kingdom’s epic stories of survival on this fast-changing and continuously evolving planet. In this Hostile Planet compilation from National Geographic, discover the animals that call deserts and the Earth’s poles home. 

Surviving the Desert - 0:00
How do animals survive in the desert? Desert wildlife relies on specialized adaptations to combat extreme heat, dehydration, and a lack of shade where the sun is the ultimate enemy. For desert animals like the Nubian ibex, Arabian wolf, and brown hyena, to survive in the desert means learning how to deal with the sun’s unrelenting volatility. 

Polar Habitats - 0:47:07
Polar habitats are similarly enslaved by the sun: half the year is plunged into bitterly cold darkness and hardship, and the other half is blistered with light and heat. What animals live in polar habitats? Polar regions are home to highly resilient species like polar bears, Arctic wolves, emperor penguins, musk ox, and more that are uniquely built to survive months of freezing darkness and sudden seasonal shifts. As the sun exerts its unquestionable dominance, we reveal the incredible ways these wild animals survive.
